passage:
'Nobody in this house gets it,' Pankaj said, dropping his bag.
Uma looked up from her laptop. 'Gets what?'
'Amma asked me to fetch vegetables. Today. When I had the worst day ever. She should know.'
'Did you tell her about the worst day?'
'She's my mother. She should just know.'
'Pankaj, she was on calls from nine to six.'
'And then Siddhu couldn't come to the ground either. Friends are supposed to be there.'
'Did you ask him?'
'I shouldn't have to ask.'
Uma closed the laptop. 'So everyone should read your mind, and when they can't, you're angry with them.'
Pankaj opened his mouth, then shut it.
'Tell me the worst day,' Uma said. 'I'm asking. Then you tell Amma at dinner.'
He sat down. 'Fine. It started with the bus.'

qa.q: How long was Amma on calls?
qa.a: Amma was on calls from nine to six.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj feel so angry that Amma asked him to fetch vegetables?
qa.a: Pankaj believes a mother should just know when her child has had a bad day, so an ordinary request feels like proof that she doesn't care.

qa.q: What turning point does Uma create, and what could Pankaj do with it?
qa.a: Uma asks to hear about the day, which shows that saying things out loud brings the understanding he wants; he could do the same with Amma at dinner and with Siddhu.

qa.q: How might Amma feel if she learned Pankaj was angry about the vegetables?
qa.a: Amma would probably be surprised and sorry, since after a long day of calls she had no way of knowing about his worst day unless he told her.

grounding: Shows a teenager who expects his mother to know his mood unasked and a friend to always be free, and grows resentful before saying a word.

passage: Looking back at Class 11, I think I was angry with almost everyone. My parents should have understood that I hated science without me saying it. Lalremsiami, my best friend, should have been free every Saturday, because that's what best friends are. When she started badminton coaching on weekends, I didn't say anything. I just got colder. I left her messages on read. I told myself she should notice. She did notice, eventually, and asked me outside the library, 'Damini, what did I do?' And I realised I'd never actually told her anything. Not about the Saturdays, not about how lonely they had got. The resentment had grown for months; the conversation took ten minutes. We moved our plans to Sunday evenings. I still catch myself thinking 'should' about people. Now it's my cue to say something.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami ask 'what did I do?'
qa.a: Lalremsiami asked outside the library.

qa.q: Why did Damini get colder instead of speaking up?
qa.a: Damini believed a best friend should just notice and be free, so saying it out loud felt like it shouldn't be needed, and the hurt turned into resentment instead.

qa.q: What does Damini do now when a 'should' thought appears, and why does it help?
qa.a: Damini treats the 'should' as a cue to say something, which catches resentment early and gives the other person a real chance to respond.

qa.q: What was it like for Lalremsiami before that talk outside the library?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt confused and shut out, watching a friend turn cold without knowing why, which is why she finally asked straight out.

grounding: Shows someone looking back on a teenage year of expecting parents and a best friend to meet unspoken needs, and resenting them when they did not.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10B, Friday
Gautam has seemed irritable all week, snapping at his group during the science project. Today he stayed back and let it out. His parents 'should understand' that he wants to switch to commerce; his friends 'should be there, every single time' for the project, and two of them went to a cousin's wedding instead. When I asked whether he had told his parents about commerce, he said, 'They should know. It's obvious.' He had not told them. He had not told his friends that the deadline worried him, either. I didn't lecture. I asked him to write three things he wished people knew, and next to each, one person he could tell. He wrote 'Papa' next to commerce. I've offered to be in the room if he wants, and I'll ask him on Monday how it went.
Nikita

qa.q: Which stream does Gautam want to switch to?
qa.a: Gautam wants to switch to commerce.

qa.q: Why does Gautam say 'They should know. It's obvious'?
qa.a: To Gautam the wish feels so clear that he believes his parents ought to see it without being told, so their silence feels unfair and feeds his irritation.

qa.q: What step did Nikita suggest, and why might it work?
qa.a: Nikita had him write three things he wished people knew and one person to tell each, which turns silent 'shoulds' into real conversations, starting with Papa.

qa.q: How might Gautam's project group see his snapping?
qa.a: The group may feel confused and hurt, since they had no idea the deadline worried him and only saw anger after two of them went to a family wedding.

grounding: Shows a teacher's note on a teenager who expects parents and friends to meet unspoken needs and grows resentful when they do not.

passage:
Friday

Papa booked the trip to Mussoorie for next weekend. The whole family. He didn't ask me. He SHOULD know I have the inter-school quiz finals that Sunday. I've been preparing for weeks. A good father would just know.

I didn't say anything at dinner. I just ate fast and left. Mummy asked if I was okay and I said "fine" in a voice that meant not fine. "Our son is sulking," she told Papa. She should have understood why.

Then I messaged Dolma to come over tomorrow and she said she has her cousin's engagement. Again. Best friends should be free when you need them. That's the whole point.

Now I'm lying here angry at everyone. Papa, Mummy, Dolma. Nobody even knows why.

...Which, okay, is maybe the problem. I didn't tell Papa about the date. I told Dolma nothing about why I needed her.

But they still should have known.

— Sahil

qa.q: What event does Sahil have on the Sunday of the trip?
qa.a: The inter-school quiz finals.

qa.q: Why does Sahil feel angry at everyone, even though nobody knows why?
qa.a: He believes his parents and Dolma should understand and be available without being told, so when they don't, he feels let down. The "should" rules make his resentment grow faster than any conversation.

qa.q: What turning point does Sahil almost reach, and what could he do next?
qa.a: He notices that he never told Papa the date or told Dolma why he needed her. Tomorrow he could tell Papa about the finals and tell Dolma what's going on, instead of waiting for them to guess.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he later learns about the quiz finals?
qa.a: Papa would likely feel surprised and sorry, wishing Sahil had told him before he booked. He might also feel hurt at being expected to guess.

grounding: A teenage boy believes his parents should know his plans and his friend should always be free, and his resentment grows faster than any conversation.

passage:
Rashmi: yash cricket nets tomorrow?
Yash: can't, helping my dad at the shop
Rashmi: you always have something
Yash: it's one saturday
Rashmi: a real friend would just be free
Yash: that's not fair
Rashmi: whatever. my parents are the same. they should know i hate tuition on sundays but nope
Yash: did you tell them?
Rashmi: i shouldn't have to tell them
Yash: ok but how would they know
Rashmi: they're my parents 😠
Yash: rashmi i'm not your parents. i'm just at the shop
Rashmi: fine
Yash: sunday evening? after your tuition?
Rashmi: seen
[Sunday, 7:10 p.m.]
Yash: still on?
Rashmi: ok. sorry for saturday. i was angry at everyone
Yash: noticed 😅 nets at 7:30

qa.q: Why couldn't Yash come to cricket nets on Saturday?
qa.a: Yash was helping Yash's dad at the shop.

qa.q: Why does Rashmi insist "I shouldn't have to tell them"?
qa.a: Rashmi feels that people who care should understand without being told, so explaining feels like proof they don't care enough. That rule turns small letdowns into resentment.

qa.q: What went wrong in the chat, and what helped fix it?
qa.a: Rashmi judged Yash by a rule that friends should always be free, which led to an unfair jab. Yash's calm offer of Sunday evening, and Rashmi's apology, turned it back into a plan.

qa.q: How might Yash feel being told a real friend would just be free?
qa.a: Yash probably felt hurt and unfairly judged, since helping at the shop wasn't a choice against Rashmi. Yash still offered another time, which shows patience.

grounding: A teenager thinks friends should always be free and parents should know without being told, and resentment builds faster than conversation.
